elements.id-string-2: \title{Ontology Enrichment from Texts: A Biomedical Dataset for Concept Discovery and Placement}
elements.id-string-15: \textit{Mentions of new concepts appear regularly in texts and require automated approaches to harvest and place them into Knowledge Bases (KB), e.g., ontologies and taxonomies.
elements.id-string-16: Existing datasets suffer from three issues, (i) mostly assuming that a new concept is pre-discovered and cannot support out-of-KB mention discovery; (ii) only using the concept label as the input along with the KB and thus lacking the contexts of a concept label; and (iii) mostly focusing on concept placement w.r.t a taxonomy of atomic concepts, instead of complex concepts, i.e., with logical operators.
elements.id-string-17: To address these issues, we propose a new benchmark, adapting MedMentions dataset (PubMed abstracts) with SNOMED CT versions in 2014 and 2017 under the Diseases sub-category and the broader categories of Clinical finding, Procedure, and Pharmaceutical / biologic product.
elements.id-string-18: We provide usage on the evaluation with the dataset for out-of-KB mention discovery and concept placement, adapting recent Large Language Model based methods.\footnote{The dataset, data construction scripts, and baseline implementation are available at \url{https://zenodo.org/record/8043690} and \url{https://github.com/KRR-Oxford/OET}.}}
elements.id-string-20: Identifying new concepts and placing them into Knowledge Bases (KBs, e.g., ontologies and taxonomies) from texts such as a vast amount of publications is a key application of AI for scientific discovery and KB construction \cite{hastings2023ai}.
elements.id-string-21: Emerging concepts are particularly common in the biomedical domain and KB can easily be outdated.
elements.id-string-22: For example, new variants of SARS-CoV-2 have kept emerging since 2020; ``Curry-Jones syndrome'' was not added to SNOMED CT ontology \cite{donnelly2006snomed} until 2017.
elements.id-string-23: Existing datasets or benchmarks on using texts to enrich ontologies, are relevant to several tasks, but each of them only reflects a part of the whole picture.

elements.id-string-26: In \textit{Ontology Extension} \cite{glauer2022interpretable}, this is extended into description logic based ontologies, which includes complex concepts which can be considered \cite{chen2023contextual,yuan2023ontolama} but not yet for the existing datasets \cite{glauer2022interpretable}.
elements.id-string-27: In \textit{Concept Post-coordination} \cite{kate2020,castell2023postcoordination}, an out-of-KB concept is defined with several existing concepts and attributes, i.e., placed under a complex concept.
elements.id-string-28: Datasets from all the three tasks above assume that the input concept term is already specified and non-contextual (e.g., without contexts in a corpus) for ontology enrichment, which does not reflect the real-world situation of discovering concepts from texts.
elements.id-string-29: In \textit{Out-of-KB Mention and Entity Discovery} \cite{Iurshina2022nilk,heist2023nastylinker,dong2023NIL}, new out-of-KB mentions and their clustering are discovered from a corpus, but their placement in KB has not been fully investigated.
elements.id-string-30: To address the issues from previous datasets, we propose a new benchmark for new entity discovery and placement, supporting two sequential tasks: (i) \textit{Out-of-KB Mention and Entity Discovery}: identifying new mentions of concepts from texts which are not included in a KB; (ii) \textit{Concept Placement}: given a \textit{new} entity expressed as a mention in the text, placing it into a KB, either an ontology with complex concepts or a taxonomy with only atomic concepts.
elements.id-string-31: Our new dataset and task setting are different from previous work in terms of the characteristics below:
elements.id-string-33: \textbf{Out-of-KB or NIL discovery}: inclusion of both in-KB and out-of-KB mentions from the texts, thus allowing the task to discover out-of-KB mentions and to place them into the KB, borrowing ideas from out-of-KB mention discovery \cite{dong2023NIL}.\textbf{Contextual terms}: inclusion of \textit{contexts} for mentions, distinct from only using concept labels as in the previous work in taxonomy completion and ontology extension.\textbf{Concept placement with complex concepts}: placement of a new term under a \textit{complex concept}, which contains at least one logical operator and distinct from previous datasets in taxonomy completion and ontology extension, which only consider atomic concepts.
elements.id-string-34: More specifically, this study uses a SNOMED CT subset as the ontology, and the time difference of two versions (in 2014 and 2017) to synthesise new entities (or KB versioning as in \cite{dong2023NIL}), then uses MedMentions Entity Linking dataset \cite{Mohan2019medmentions} (from PubMed abstracts to UMLS) to construct in-KB and out-of-KB mentions w.r.t.

elements.id-string-71: In this work, we present dataset construction for \textit{\textbf{Concept Discovery and Placement}} to support a comprehensive set of characteristics (Table \ref{dataset-summary}), with usage for benchmarking, e.g., with LLMs.
elements.id-string-73: The task of \textit{Concept Discovery and Placement} inputs contextual, in-KB and out-of-KB mentions in a corpus and a KB (more formally as an OWL ontology \cite{GRAU2008OWL2,baader_horrocks_lutz_sattler_2017chap8}) and outputs an enriched KB where each out-of-KB mention is inserted into a \textit{directed edge}, i.e., $<\texttt{parent, child}>$, of the KB, when the out-of-KB mention is the child of the \texttt{parent} and the parent of the \texttt{child}.
elements.id-string-74: The \texttt{child} is considered NULL when the mention corresponds to a leaf concept.
elements.id-string-76: Several key definitions are as follows.
elements.id-string-77: Formally, an \textit{OWL ontology} is a Description Logic KB that contains a set of axioms \cite{GRAU2008OWL2,baader_horrocks_lutz_sattler_2017chap8}.
elements.id-string-78: We focus on the TBox (or the terminology part) in an ontology, which mainly consists of General Concept Inclusion axioms of the form $A \sqsubseteq B$, where $A$ (and $B$) are either atomic or complex concepts \cite{baader_horrocks_lutz_sattler_2017chap2}.
elements.id-string-79: A TBox can be reduced to a \textit{taxonomy} (or a subsumption hierarchy) after the classification process \cite{baader_horrocks_lutz_sattler_2017chap2}.
elements.id-string-80: Borrowing the definition of taxonomy in \cite{Jiang2022taxoenrich,Shen2020TaxoExpan}, we use a simple definition of ontology as a set of concepts and directed edges, where both can be atomic or complex.
elements.id-string-81: \textit{Directed Edges} are edges in an ontology (or a taxonomy \cite{Wang2022QEN}) which contain a direct parent and a direct child.
elements.id-string-82: \textit{Complex edges} are edges which have a complex concept as the parent\footnote{It is not likely to have complex concepts as direct (asserted) children in anontology.}.
elements.id-string-83: \textit{Complex concepts} mean concepts that involve at least one logical operators, e.g., negation ($\neg$), conjunction ($\sqcap$), disjunction ($\sqcup$), existential restriction ($\exists r.C$), universal restriction ($\forall r.
elements.id-string-85: \cite{baader_horrocks_lutz_sattler_2017chap2}.\footnote{The OWL ontology language \cite{GRAU2008OWL2}, based on Description Logic, has expressiveness beyond traditional RDF triples \cite{baader_horrocks_lutz_sattler_2017chap8}; an example complex concept as a parent concept is $Arthritis \sqsubseteq Arthropathy \sqcap \exists hasMorphology.Inflammatory$, which is not easily expressed with a single RDF triple \cite{yuan2023ontolama}.}

elements.id-string-88: An ideal dataset for \textit{Concept Discovery and Placement} requires a real-world text corpus and a large OWL ontology (reducible to a taxonomy), with gold-standard directed edges (possibly complex) for each out-of-KB concept linked to the mentions in the corpus.
elements.id-string-91: We consider SNOMED CT \cite{donnelly2006snomed}, one of the most important OWL ontology in the biomedical domain, and choose a subset by selected categories of concepts.
elements.id-string-92: We focus on the second level category, \textit{Disease} (disorder) and the first level categories, \textit{Clinical finding}, \textit{Pharmaceutical / biologic product}, and \textit{Procedure}, abbreviated to \textit{CPP} as the initials of the categories.
elements.id-string-93: CPP categories have the most important types of complex edges for placement (or post-coordination), according to \citet{kate2020}.
elements.id-string-94: The subset selection has two steps: (i) transforming equivalence axioms into subsumption axioms by outermost conjunctions, e.g., from $A \equiv C_1 \sqcap \exists R.(C_2 \sqcap C_3)$ to $A \sqsubseteq C_1$ and $A \sqsubseteq \exists R.(C_2 \sqcap C_3)$; (ii) pruning the ontology to only keep the selected categories.\footnote{Given that many subsumption relations are in fact described as equivalence axioms with conjunction with concepts from to-be-removed categories, simply using step (ii) without step (i) will result in many broken hierarchies instead of a connected one.}
elements.id-string-96: First, we transform SNOMED CT files\footnote{\url{https://www.nlm.nih.gov/healthit/snomedct/archive.html}} into OWL format with snomed-owl-toolkit\footnote{\url{https://github.com/IHTSDO/snomed-owl-toolkit}}.
elements.id-string-97: Then, step (i) is implemented through ontology processing with DeepOnto\footnote{\url{https://github.com/KRR-Oxford/DeepOnto}} and step (ii) is carried out with Protégé\footnote{\url{http://protegeproject.github.io/protege/}} to remove the other categories.
elements.id-string-99: We follow a KB versioning strategy \cite{dong2023NIL,Iurshina2022nilk} to synthesise out-of-KB entities for the older KB.
elements.id-string-100: The concept gap between the two versions of SNOMED CT subsets (ver 20140901 and 20170301) is considered.
elements.id-string-101: The numbers of concepts in the older and the newer sub-KB are 64,800 and 72,595, resp., for the \textit{Disease} sub-category and are 175,895 and 188,988, resp., for \textit{CPP} categories.
elements.id-string-103: We extract the directed edges in the older sub-KB for both in-KB and out-of-KB entities.
elements.id-string-104: For in-KB entities, this is achieved by querying all the direct parents and children in the older KB.
elements.id-string-105: For out-of-KB entities, this is achieved by queries all the \textit{most} direct, in-KB (older KB) parents and children from the newer sub-KB, given that edges for the out-of-KB entities are not available in the older KB.
elements.id-string-106: If the entity is a leaf node, we set the direct child as NULL, as in \citet{zhang2021TMN}.
elements.id-string-107: The querying process is based on the ontology processing module in DeepOnto, which is based on OWL API \cite{horridge2011owl}.
elements.id-string-109: A corpus with mentions linked to entities in SNOMED CT is needed to synthesise contextual mentions and gold-standard edges.
elements.id-string-110: Following \citet{dong2023NIL}, we use MedMentions\footnote{\url{https://github.com/chanzuckerberg/MedMentions}} \cite{Mohan2019medmentions}, containing around 5,000 biomedical paper abstracts in PubMed\footnote{https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/} where the mentions were manually and exhaustively linked to UMLS \cite{Bodenreider2004umls} (version 2017AA)\footnote{There are also other datasets available, e.g. COMETA \cite{basaldella2020cometa}, which directly links mentions in social media posts on Reddit to SNOMED CT.
elements.id-string-111: Still, we consider scientific publications a more reliable source and leave social media for a future study.}.
elements.id-string-112: We leverage the alignment of entities in UMLS to obtain  SNOMED CT entities (ver 20170301)\footnote{If mention of one UMLS entity matches to multiple SNOMED CT entities, we create a mention row in the data for each SNOMED CT entity.}.
elements.id-string-113: Using the output from the previous steps, we can then map each in-KB and out-of-KB mention to edges\footnote{We also filtered the edges to one hop (including leaf concept to NULL) and two hops for the out-of-KB mentions.} in the older sub-KB (SNOMED CT ver 20140901).
elements.id-string-114: We thus create mention-to-edge datasets with the information for each mention, each rendered in a JSON format.
elements.id-string-115: The information includes the left and the right contexts of the mention ($\text{ctxt}_l$ and $\text{ctxt}_r$), the mention or concept itself and its SNOMED CT ID, the parent and child in the older SNOMED CT ID (and with expression for complex concepts) and their labels.\footnote{The keys in the JSON format are available in \url{https://github.com/KRR-Oxford/OET}.} We use DeepOnto's verbaliser \cite{yuan2023ontolama} to form labels of the complex concepts.
elements.id-string-116: Regarding data splitting for the benchmark, for \textit{out-of-KB mention and concept discovery}, the dataset follows the original splits of training, validation, and testing sets from MedMentions; for \textit{concept placement}, the setting is unsupervised for out-of-KB mentions, i.e., training (and validating) with in-KB mentions but testing on out-of-KB mentions (and in-KB mentions).

elements.id-string-125: \subsubsection*{Metrics for Out-of-KB Mention Discovery} The dataset supports the metrics in \cite{dong2023NIL}, including overall accuracy for all in-KB and out-of-KB mentions ($A$); \textit{out-of-KB} precision ($P_o$), recall ($R_o$), and $F_1$ score ($F_{1_o}$) to measure how well out-of-KB mentions are detected; and \textit{in-KB} precision ($P_{in}$), recall ($R_{in}$, and $F_1$ score ($F_{1_{in}}$).
elements.id-string-126: \subsubsection*{Metrics for Concept Placement} The dataset supports the metrics used in taxonomy completion, to evaluate the ranking of edges for a given mention \cite{zhang2021TMN,Jiang2022taxoenrich,Shen2020TaxoExpan}.
elements.id-string-127: The metrics mainly include Precision at $k$ (P@$k$), Recall at $k$ (R@$k$), $F_1$ score at $k$ ($F_1$@$k$), Mean Rank (MR), and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR).
elements.id-string-128: We report P@$k$ and R@$k$ for different top-$k$ values.
elements.id-string-130: We experiment with the data w.r.t the two tasks using a rule-based method and recent, LLM-based methods.
elements.id-string-136: \subsubsection*{For Out-of-KB Mention Discovery} Existing methods are supervised, i.e., require a certain amount of NIL in the training data.
elements.id-string-137: Thus, we split the ``out-of-KB'' mentions in Table \ref{data-statistics} based on the NIL mentions in the original MedMentions data split.
elements.id-string-138: The number of training, validation, and testing NIL mentions are 568, 260, and 172, resp., for CPP (in total 1,000 mentions); and 329, 161, and 115, resp., for Disease sub-categories  (in total 605 mentions).
elements.id-string-139: For the rule-based method, we use the Sieve-based approach, which uses rules designed for biomedical texts and predicts a mention as out-of-KB if no in-KB entity can be linked to \cite{dsouza-ng-2015-sieve-based}.
elements.id-string-140: For the LLM-based method, we follow BLINKout \cite{dong2023NIL} to detect out-of-KB mentions from texts adapting a two-step BERT-based approach \cite{wu2020blink}: candidate generation with bi-encoder and candidate selection with cross-encoder.
elements.id-string-141: Out-of-KB mentions are discovered through NIL entity representation and classification in the cross-encoder \cite{dong2023NIL}.
elements.id-string-142: Default parameters are used, with top-$k$ value as 50, the domain-specific, SapBERT model \cite{liu2021sap}.
elements.id-string-143: \subsubsection*{Results on Out-of-KB Mention Discovery} Table \ref{out-of-KB-res} shows that BLINKout performs much better than the Sieve-based approach in terms of the overall accuracy and out-of-KB $F_1$ scores.
elements.id-string-144: However, it is still challenging to achieve satisfying performance to identify out-of-KB mentions (with out-of-KB $F_{1}$ between 15\% and 30\%).
elements.id-string-145: \subsubsection*{For Concept Placement} We use the mention-edge pairs (see Table \ref{data-statistics}) to train and validate a model to match an \textit{in-KB} mention to its gold-standard directed edges in a KB and then test on \textit{out-of-KB} mentions, following the unsupervised setting.
elements.id-string-146: The model architecture includes edge candidate generation with an optional step of edge selection.
elements.id-string-147: For edge candidate generation, we adapt the bi-encoder  \cite{wu2020blink}, with the input of a contextual mention and an edge  (i.e., edge-bi-encoder), to match a contextual mention to a directed edge in an ontology using their concept names\footnote{An edge is represented as ``parent tokens \texttt{[P-TAG]} child tokens \texttt{[C-TAG]}''.}.
elements.id-string-148: Top-$k$ edges rankings are selected after this step.
elements.id-string-149: For an optional edge selection among the top-$k$, we test the capability of zero-shot prompting of an LLM, GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo), where $k$ is set as 50.
elements.id-string-150: The prompt includes a header, the mention with contexts, and the top-$k$ candidate edges to query the LLM to select the correct edges\footnote{Further details, parameter settings, and prompts of the experiments are available at \url{https://github.com/KRR-Oxford/OET}.}.
elements.id-string-152: Table \ref{insertion-res} suggests that concept placement as edge prediction is very challenging.
elements.id-string-153: Also, using GPT-3.5 to select top-1 from the top-50 edge candidates does not improve, or only improves marginally, the results with the prompts.
elements.id-string-154: The benchmark's result may suggest the limitation of the state-of-the-art LLM interacting with formal, domain-specific knowledge using zero-shot prompting.
elements.id-string-156: This work introduced a new benchmark for Ontology Enrichment from Texts by Concept Discovery and Placement.
elements.id-string-157: The dataset focuses on enriching OWL ontologies as formal KBs, which are reducible to and thus compatible with taxonomies.
elements.id-string-158: Compared to the prior art, the dataset supports a more comprehensive set of characteristics, including NIL Discovery, Contextual Term, Concept Placement, and Complex Concepts.
elements.id-string-159: We propose a pipeline to construct this resource and release a dataset using MedMentions corpus (PubMed abstracts), UMLS and SNOMED CT ontologies.
elements.id-string-160: We provide usage of the data by evaluating recent LLM-based methods.
elements.id-string-161: The data construction method can be applied to other KBs in the biomedical domain and KBs in various domains.
elements.id-string-162: The baseline LLM-based methods are yet to achieve satisfying performance on the benchmark.
elements.id-string-163: Further methods are encouraged to address this challenge.

elements.id-string-182: In this study, we propose a new benchmark for new entity discovery and placement, supporting two sequential tasks: (i) \textit{Out-of-KB Mention and Entity Discovery}: identifying new mentions of concepts from texts which are not included in a KB; (ii) \textit{Concept Placement}: given a \textit{new} entity expressed as a mention in the text, placing it into a KB, either an ontology with complex concepts or a taxonomy with only atomic concepts.
elements.id-string-183: \textbf{Out-of-KB or NIL discovery}: inclusion of \textit{out-of-KB mentions} from texts to support their concept discovery and placement.\textbf{Contextual terms}: inclusion of \textit{contexts} for mentions, distinct from only using concept labels as in the previous work.\textbf{Complex concepts}: placement of concepts under logic-equipped \textit{complex concepts}, instead of atomic concepts alone.
elements.id-string-184: More specifically, the study uses a SNOMED CT subset as the ontology, and the time difference of two versions (in 2014 and 2017) to synthesise new entities, then uses MedMentions Entity Linking dataset \cite{Mohan2019medmentions} (from PubMed abstracts to UMLS) to construct in-KB and out-of-KB mentions.
elements.id-string-185: The study further introduces the usage of the data with evaluation for out-of-KB mention discovery and concept placement.
